introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education (GCE) Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0560), Paper 2 - Modern World History Since 1870, ORDINARY LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR Questions. TWO questions must be chosen from SECTION A, ONE from SECTION B and ONE other from SECTION C. One of the two questions chosen from SECTION A must be a Starred question.

Maps should be used to illustrate answers where appropriate. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION A: CAMEROON SINCE 1850**

Question ONE is compulsory. Answer either 1A* or 1B* and one other Question from this section.

**Or**

**B\* (Starred question)** *Study these two extracts under the Ahidjo and Biya Administrations and then answer questions (a) to (e) which follow. (The maximum mark for each sub question is indicated in brackets)*

*(The extracts are set line by line as printed; the line numbers printed in the right margin are shown in square brackets. The dotted gaps are as printed.)*

> **Extract A:** The moves towards the Federation of East and West Cameroon was cemented by President Ahidjo  
> on 1st September 1961 when he signed into law an important Constitution. The Constitution took effect on......  
> According to the Constitution, the President was both Head of State and Head of Government............ The  
> Republic of Cameroon reunified with...... In the year...... with Charles Assale as first Prime Minister of the  
> Federated State of East Cameroon with headquarters in Yaounde. The most serious threats to the Ahijos regime [5]  
> in East Cameroon came from a political party with an exiled wing, which was too militant.  
> The political base of Ahidjo was still very narrow in 1960 and his UC party had only 31 out of the 70 seats in  
> the East Cameroon House of Assembly. To strengthen his political base Ahidjo exploited the rift within the  
> Opposition camp in East Cameroon to form a Unified Party through subjugation, bribery, and corruption.  
> The politics in West Cameroon was more complex but democratic. Ahidjo decided to seek political alliance [10]  
> with the political parties in West Cameroon to have a total grip on political power and by the mid-1960s  
> Cameroon had become a One Party State.

> **Extract B:** Paul Biya inherited that political party when he came to power in 1982 but as a result of political  
> disagreement that necessitated the holding of a party congress at Bamenda in March 1985, a **new** name was  
> adopted for that single party of the country. Between 1986 and 1990, international and national pressure was [15]  
> brought to bear on him because of the wing of change blowing from Eastern Europe following the introduction  
> of the policies of **Glasnot** and **Perestroika** and because of the growing demand for political reforms at home.  
> Biya was forced to sign a legislation initiating a series of liberal political reforms in December 1990 that saw  
> the rebirth of multi- party politics in which hundreds of political parties came into existence in Cameroon.

**Source:** *Adapted from Victor Julius Ngoh: Cameroon 1884-Present (2018). The History of a People.*
incertitudes: Question 1B : les deux extraits sont recopiés ligne par ligne comme imprimé (numérotation 5, 10, 15 conservée ; les lignes 1 à 12 pour l'extrait A, 13 à 15 et suivantes pour l'extrait B), car les sous-questions renvoient aux lignes 2, 3, 4, 6, 11 et 12. Fautes d'impression conservées : « Ahijos », « Glasnot », « wing of change », « multi- party », « Assale », « Yaounde », « 4 marks » collé (« 1+4marks »), « mentioned in line 6.. » (ramené à un seul point dans l'énoncé de (c)) ; les blancs « ...... » de l'extrait A (date d'entrée en vigueur, territoire réunifié, année, fonctions) sont imprimés tels quels dans le sujet.

1B (a)(i) : le « nom populaire » de la Constitution est donné comme « Federal Constitution » (aussi « Foumban Constitution ») ; le corrigé officiel attend probablement « Federal Constitution ». 1B (a)(ii) : entrée en vigueur en octobre 1961 (le 1er octobre) ; 1B (a)(iii) : fonctions du Président de la Fédération données dans leurs grandes lignes, sans numéro d'article.

1B (b)(i) : la lecture retenue est « Southern Cameroons » (devenu « West Cameroon ») ; la ligne 4 de l'extrait ne cite que les blancs et l'État fédéré de l'Est, la question vise le territoire qui s'est réuni à la République. 1B (c)(i) : les partis d'Est-Cameroun qui ont rejoint le parti unifié (PSC, PDC) sont donnés d'après l'historiographie courante, le corrigé officiel peut en citer d'autres ; 1B (c)(ii) : la lecture retenue est l'UPC et, pour le chef de l'aile en exil, Félix-Roland Moumié (mort en novembre 1960), ce qui laisse la possibilité que le corrigé officiel attende un autre nom (Abel Kingué, Ernest Ouandié) ; question la moins sûre de 1B.

1B (d)(i) : partis de l'Ouest-Cameroun cités d'après l'historiographie courante (CPNC, CUC) ; 1B (d)(ii) : 1966 (création de l'UNC en septembre 1966). 1B (e)(ii) : la question renvoie à « the political party cited in c(i) above », renvoi erroné (la bonne référence est e(i)) ; le corrigé répond sur le parti adopté à Bamenda en 1985 (RDPC / CPDM). Les raisons du maintien au pouvoir sont celles de l'analyse courante, formulées sans chiffre ; sujet politiquement sensible, à relire.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a)

(i) By what popular name is the Constitution mentioned in line 2 of the extract called?

(ii) Give both the **month** and the **year** the Constitution cited in a (i) above came into effect.

(iii) Give **two** functions of the Head of State and Government in line 3 of the extract.

**(1+2+2 marks)**

(b)

(i) What name was given to the territory that reunited with the Republic of Cameroon in line 4 of the extract.

(ii) At the time of reunification who was the Prime Minister of the territory in b (i) above and the political party he headed?

(iii) Which town served as headquarters of the territory cited in b (i) above?

**(1 + 2 + 1 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The territory (1 mark).** **Southern Cameroons**, the British-administered territory which voted to join the Republic of Cameroon in the plebiscite of 11 February 1961. After the reunification of 1 October 1961 it became the **Federated State of West Cameroon**.

**(ii) Prime Minister and party (2 marks).** The Prime Minister was **John Ngu Foncha** (1 mark), who headed the **Kamerun National Democratic Party (KNDP)** (1 mark). At the reunification Foncha became Vice-President of the Federal Republic, and A.N. Jua succeeded him as Prime Minister of West Cameroon in 1965.

**(iii) Headquarters (1 mark).** **Buea**, the capital of Southern Cameroons and then of the Federated State of West Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c)

(i) Name **one** political group in East Cameroon that willingly accepted to join Ahidjo in the formation of a Unified Party.

(ii) Give the name of the opposing party to Ahidjo's idea of a Unified Party and the leader of the exiled wing of the militant party mentioned in line 6.

**(1+2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A group that joined Ahidjo (1 mark).** Any one of the East Cameroon parties that merged with Ahidjo's Union Camerounaise (UC) to form the Cameroon National Union (UNC) in 1966, for example the **Parti Socialiste Camerounais (PSC)** or the **Parti des Démocrates Camerounais (PDC)**, in the process of building the single party between 1961 and 1966.

**(ii) The opposing party and the exiled leader (2 marks).** The party that opposed the idea of a Unified Party, and whose exiled wing was "too militant" (line 6), was the **Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC)**. The exiled wing was led by **Félix-Roland Moumié** (President of the UPC, assassinated in Geneva in November 1960), and after his death by other leaders such as **Abel Kingué**; **Ernest Ouandié** led the maquis inside the country.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d)

(i) Give the name of **two** political parties mentioned in line 11 that operated in West Cameroon at the time other than the party demanded in b (ii) above.

(ii) Give the year in which Cameroon became a One Party State as mentioned in line 12.

**(2 + 1 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two other West Cameroon parties (2 marks).** The party "demanded in b (ii)" is the KNDP. Two other parties of West Cameroon at the time (1 mark each): the **Cameroon People's National Convention (CPNC)** and the **Cameroon United Congress (CUC)**. (The One Kamerun party and the Kamerun Peoples Party were also active in the early 1960s.)

**(ii) The year of the One Party State (1 mark).** **1966.** On 1 September 1966 the parties of East and West Cameroon merged with Ahidjo's UC into the **Cameroon National Union (UNC)**, which ended multi-party politics.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e)

(i) Identify the new party adopted during the Bamenda Congress in March 1985.

(ii) Why has the political party cited in c(i) above remained in power for so long?

**(1+4marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The new party (1 mark).** The **Cameroon People's Democratic Movement (CPDM)**, in French the *Rassemblement Démocratique du Peuple Camerounais (RDPC)*, which replaced the Cameroon National Union at the Bamenda Congress of March 1985.

**(ii) Why it has stayed in power so long (4 marks).** (The sheet says "the party cited in c(i)", but c(i) only asks for parties that joined Ahidjo; the question clearly means the party of e(i), the CPDM.) Reasons commonly given (any four, one mark each, explained):

1. **Control of the state apparatus.** The party inherited the single party's structures and resources; the administration, governors, prefects and the public service are tied to the ruling party, and the President appoints the main office holders.
2. **A divided and weak opposition.** After the multi-party reforms of December 1990, hundreds of parties appeared but they were fragmented, short of money and unable to unite behind one candidate.
3. **Control of elections.** The opposition denounces the organisation and results of elections, the electoral register and the role of the administration, and many elections have been boycotted by part of the opposition.
4. **Patronage and ethnic balancing.** Offices and public resources are shared among regions and elites to build support and to win over rivals.
5. **The security forces and the law.** Public order laws and the police have been used to limit demonstrations and opposition meetings.
6. **Constitutional changes.** The 1996 Constitution and the 2008 amendment, which removed the limit on the number of presidential terms, allowed the head of the party to remain President.
7. **Stability argument.** Supporters present the party as the guarantee of peace and stability in a region marked by conflicts.
